summary: This Cerebral Cortex article (Petkoski, Ritter, Jirsa, 2023) analyzes diffusion MRI and fMRI from 50 adults aged 18 to 80 to show how age-related white-matter loss shapes brain connectivity. The authors find the largest tract loss in frontal regions and for long inter-hemispheric links, and they use a Kuramoto-oscillator whole-brain model to test whether compensation and demyelination-driven slowing of propagation velocity explain age-related functional changes. The note covers the introduction, methods, and first results, including lobe-specific tract count and length correlations with age.
one_line: Study of how age-related white-matter degradation and dynamical compensation shape functional connectivity in adult human brains, tested with a whole-brain oscillator model.
key_facts: The article was published in Cerebral Cortex, Volume 33, Issue 10, 15 May 2023, pages 6241–6256, with DOI 10.1093/cercor/bhac500.
The authors are Spase Petkoski, Petra Ritter, and Viktor K Jirsa.
The study analyzed anatomical and diffusion-weighted images of 50 subjects acquired at Berlin Center for Advanced Imaging, Charité University Medicine, Berlin, Germany.
The subjects ranged in age from 18 to 80 years, with a mean age of 41.26 and 30 females and 20 males.
The Desikan–Killiany atlas as implemented in FREESURFER yielded 68 cortical regions of interest.
The largest decrease of streamlines was found in frontal regions and for long inter-hemispheric links.
The model tested the hypotheses that demyelination has no impact on propagation velocity or decreases it by 30% and 50%.

The abstract states that age-related functional fingerprints are only supported if the model accounts for compensation for overall loss of structural connectivity and a decrease of propagation velocity due to loss of myelination.
Static FC features did not show significant differences with age, while dFC showed more stable dynamics and MC showed a wider range and variance.
The Kuramoto model in the study has 68 delay-coupled cortical regions, with the global coupling G and the age-dependent mean axonal propagation velocity as the only free hyper-parameters explored.
Dynamic functional connectivity was computed for four window sizes: 30, 15, 10, and 5 time points.
The frontal lobe was the most affected by the decrease of fiber counts, according to Table 1 (top).
Mean and median tract lengths decrease with aging, and the external and long links are mostly affected.
The Louvain algorithm from the Brain Connectivity Toolbox was used for community detection on weighted undirected links, with modularity computed for partitions of 2, 3, 4, and 5 communities.
Simulated neural activity was converted to BOLD signals using the Balloon–Windkessel model of The Virtual Brain.
